bibliography.title: CyberGym: Evaluating AI Agents' Real-World Cybersecurity Capabilities at Scale

sections.title: 5 From Benchmarking to Direct Security Impact
A. The Use of Large Language Models
E. Analysis of Incomplete Patches and Zero-day Vulnerabilities

abstract_sentences.text: AI agents have significant potential to reshape cybersecurity, making a thorough assessment of their capabilities critical.

evidence.anchor: assessment of their capabilities critical

abstract_sentences.text: However, existing evaluations fall short, because they are based on small-scale benchmarks and only measure static outcomes, failing to capture the full, dynamic range of real-world security challenges.

evidence.anchor: small-scale benchmarks and only measure static outcomes

abstract_sentences.text: To address these limitations, we introduce CyberGym, a large-scale benchmark featuring 1,507 real-world vulnerabilities across 188 software projects.

evidence.anchor: 1,507 real-world vulnerabilities across 188 software projects

abstract_sentences.text: Adjustable to different vulnerability analysis settings, CyberGym primarily tasks agents with generating a proof-of-concept test that reproduces a vulnerability, given only its text description and the corresponding codebase.

evidence.anchor: generating a proof-of-concept test

abstract_sentences.text: Our extensive evaluation highlights that CyberGym effectively differentiates agents’ and models’ cybersecurity capabilities.

evidence.anchor: effectively differentiates agents’ and models’

abstract_sentences.text: Even the top-performing combinations only achieve a ∼20% success rate, demonstrating the overall difficulty of CyberGym.

evidence.anchor: only achieve a ∼20% success rate

abstract_sentences.text: Beyond static benchmarking, we show that CyberGym leads to the discovery of 34 zero-day vulnerabilities and 18 historically incomplete patches.

evidence.anchor: 34 zero-day vulnerabilities and 18 historically incomplete patches

abstract_sentences.text: These results underscore that CyberGym is not only a robust benchmark for measuring AI’s progress in cybersecurity but also a platform for creating direct, real-world security impact.

evidence.anchor: platform for creating direct, real-world security impact

experimental_design.description: Section 4 uses directional headings but does not pre-list numbered hypotheses, preregistered thresholds or stopping rules.

experimental_design.name: benchmark population and dates

experimental_design.name: primary task and oracle
experimental_design.description: Level 1 supplies vulnerability description and pre-patch codebase/executable; success requires pre-patch sanitizer crash and post-patch no sanitizer crash.

experimental_design.name: LLM cohort
experimental_design.description: Eleven LLMs span six closed-source general models, two open-weight general models and three SWE-bench-specialized models.

experimental_design.description: OpenHands, Codex CLI, EnIGMA and Cybench are compared; LLM comparison uses OpenHands, framework comparison uses GPT-4.1.

result_inventory.claim: Generated PoCs reveal post-patch crashes and zero-days.
result_inventory.value: 759 post-patch crashes across 60 projects; 35 still crash on latest versions; manual root-cause analysis/dedup yields 9 unique zero-days; average confirmed duration 969 days.

result_inventory.statistical_method: Execution counts plus manual root-cause analysis and deduplication; no public per-case false-positive table.

final_judgment.single_storyline: OSS-Fuzz historical vulnerabilities plus pre/post sanitizer execution produce a 1,507-instance PoC-reproduction benchmark; post-patch replay and Level-0 search extend the benchmark to incomplete patches and zero-day discovery. [p. 4–10, §§3–5]
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main text retains task input/output, the two-condition oracle, Level 0–3, dataset scale, 4 agents/11 LLMs, Figures 3–7, one successful Figure 8 trace and the §5 discovery pipeline. [p. 4–10]
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Prompts, README, hardware, checkpoints/commits, full project/crash-type tables, resampling, failure ratios, long traces and the GDAL/zero-day summary are in p. 16–46; headline benchmark remains readable, while audit of configuration and impact requires the appendix. [p. 16–46]
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 1’s input→oracle→impact chain followed by the explicit pre/post criterion and model/information/length comparisons gives a clear executable-to-impact progression. [p. 2, 4–8]
final_judgment.largest_gap: The 34-zero-day and 18-incomplete-patch claims depend on manual root-cause/deduplication and disclosure-limited case evidence; introduction counts 17/10 while §5 gives 18/9, and proxy calibration covers only two models. [p. 2, 9–11]
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For agent benchmarks, keep task input, executable success oracle, denominator, one mechanism trace, key heterogeneity/failure diagnostic and the impact decision in the main text; move long logs and full configuration to a called appendix. [p. 4–10, 19–46]
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule fits reproduction tasks with a credible pre/post execution oracle. Logic flaws, exploitation, patch preservation, web/mobile tasks and human evaluation need distinct validity oracles and mechanism evidence. [p. 4, 10]

lexical_profile.scope: Main prose p1–10; references excluded; morphology and case variants merged for semantic labels; figures/tables/traces can leave residual labels.
lexical_profile.interpretation: Strong numeric claim verbs cluster in Abstract/§4/§5; weaker or qualified verbs cluster in scope, contamination discussion and future work. The trace tokens mng_LOOP, ReadMNGImage, grep/ls/find and et al. are context-specific, not theory terms.
